text: This page compares the skills most commonly requested in our filtered apparel and fashion analytics job postings with the team’s current skill levels, highlighting where the team is well-positioned and where gaps remain.

title: Skill Gap Analysis
text:
Most In-Demand Skills
Skill fields were parsed from each posting’s listed skills. Counts reflect how many of the 19 filtered postings mention each skill at least once.


                            
                                            


We pulled the skills listed in each posting and counted how often each one showed up across our 19 filtered postings. Power BI and SQL came out on top with 7 postings each. Python and Microsoft Excel followed with 5 postings each and Digital Marketing appeared in 4. The remaining skills each appeared in 2 to 3 postings, reflecting a mix of technical, analytical, and communication skills expected across these roles.

title: Skill Gap Analysis
text:
Team Skill Comparison
Each team member self-rated their proficiency on the eight most in-demand skills identified above using a scale from 1 (Beginner) to 5 (Expert).


                            
                                            




                            
                                            


As a team we rated ourselves strongest in Data Analysis and Excel with average scores of 4.0 and 4.25 which reflects consistent comfort across all four members. Power BI and Python came in lowest at an average of 2.75 each putting both just below Intermediate as a team. Digital Marketing showed the widest range of any skill running from 2 (Beginner) to 4 (Advanced) which reflects how varied our backgrounds are on that front.

title: Skill Gap Analysis
text:
Skill Gaps
Comparing market demand against team proficiency helps show where we’re well-covered and where the gaps actually are both as a team and for each of us individually.
As a team Power BI is our largest gap. It’s tied for the most in-demand skill in the market showing up in 7 of 19 postings but has the lowest average proficiency on the team at 2.75. SQL is the other most requested skill at 7 of 19 postings and fares a bit better with a team average of 3.25. Python is requested in 5 postings and also comes in low at 2.75. Excel and Data Analysis are the opposite story: both are in demand in the market and also where we rate ourselves strongest so there’s no real gap to address there.
Breaking this down by person the picture looks a bit different for each of us:

Alyssa rates Intermediate (3) in Power BI SQL and Python the three most in-demand technical skills and rates strongest in Data Analysis Stakeholder Management and Project Management (all 4). Power BI and SQL are her clearest priorities since they’re the two most requested skills in the market and she’s only at Intermediate in both.
Ankita follows a similar pattern also rating a 3 in Power BI SQL and Python with Digital Marketing as her lowest rating (2). Since Power BI and SQL have the highest market demand those are the higher priority gaps for her compared to Digital Marketing.
Sara has the largest individual gap in Power BI rating herself a 2 (Beginner) the lowest score on the team for the most in-demand skill and she’s also lowest on Python (2). She’s strongest in Excel (5) and rates highly in Digital Marketing Stakeholder Management and Data Analysis (all 4).
Zech has the strongest overall technical profile on the team rating Advanced (4) in SQL Project Management and Data Analysis. His lowest ratings are Power BI and Digital Marketing (both 3) making Power BI his one real gap relative to the market’s top-requested skill.

title: Skill Gap Analysis
text:
Improvement Plan
Based on the gaps above our individual priorities are:

Alyssa and Ankita should prioritize Power BI and SQL since both are currently at Intermediate despite being the two most requested skills in the market. Microsoft’s free Power BI learning path along with practicing SQL queries against the team’s own filtered dataset would tie skill-building directly to the project.
Sara should prioritize Power BI first since it’s the team’s lowest individual rating on the market’s most in-demand skill followed by Python. Given her existing strength in Excel a Power BI path that builds on familiar spreadsheet concepts (for example Microsoft’s Excel-to-Power-BI transition materials) may be the fastest route in.
Zech should prioritize Power BI the one skill where his rating trails his otherwise strong technical profile. Given his existing SQL proficiency focusing on Power BI’s data modeling features is a natural next step since those build on relational concepts he already knows.

Across the team Power BI is the most consistent gap since every member rated it at 3 or below while it ties for the highest market demand. Team members with relatively higher proficiency in a given skill (for example Zech in SQL and Sara in Excel) can informally support others when related project tasks come up rather than treating skill-building as separate from the coursework itself.

title: Career Pathway and Industry Scope
text:
Target career pathway: Business/Data Analyst roles
Industry code: NAICS 458 (Clothing, Clothing Accessories, Shoe, and Jewelry Retailers), within the broader apparel and fashion retail sector
Industry label: Apparel and Fashion Retail

title: Career Pathway and Industry Scope
text:
Research Rationale
Business and data analysts turn operational data into decisions organizations can act on. Apparel retail is a good place to study that work, since retailers are constantly reacting to seasonal demand, shifting consumer preferences, inventory limits, pricing calls, and supply chain pressure. Those conditions give analytical skills a direct, visible role in how the business runs.
For a student weighing an analytics career, it is not always obvious which skills employers actually care about, or whether their coursework and experience line up with what the job market expects. A title like “business analyst” or “data analyst” hides a lot of variation: some mix of technical ability, analytical thinking, communication, and business judgment, and the exact mix shifts by employer. This project tries to pin down which skills matter most for business/data analyst roles in apparel retail specifically, then checks that list against our own team’s current skills.
That is what separates this from a plain labor-market summary: it is meant to work as a career evaluation tool. A student should be able to look at it and see what employers are asking for, where their own strengths already line up, and what still needs work before they apply.

title: Career Pathway and Industry Scope
text:
Literature Review
Umamaheswaran et al. (2023) looked at what employers ask for in business analytics postings and found a consistent mix: big data, business intelligence, and analytical technique on one side, communication and stakeholder management on the other. That matters for how we think about readiness. Knowing the software is not enough on its own; an analyst also has to understand the business problem and explain results to people who are not going to read the code.
Alshameri & Adhikari (2025) looked at business job postings the same way and identified the same kind of gap. Employers ask for a mix of general tools like Microsoft Office and data visualization plus skills specific to their field and the exact mix depends on industry and location. The study refers to this as a growing disconnect between what schools teach and what employers are actually looking for. In addition Debortoli et al. (2014) conducted a comparable analysis of business intelligence and big data postings and found the same pattern. Employers separate technical tool skills from broader analytical thinking and the strongest candidates show both.
Apparel retail is a fitting test case for that combination. Forecasting, inventory, pricing, and supply chain decisions all show up as recurring analytical needs in clothing retail, and IBISWorld (2025) backs that up with broader industry context on clothing and clothing accessory retailers. Demand in this sector moves fast and shifts with the seasons, which is part of why data-supported decisions carry more weight here than they might in a slower-moving industry.
Fashion retail has been leaning harder into data analytics in recent years. Oh (2020) found that fashion brands increasingly use data analytics to personalize products plan merchandising and improve profitability and argued that education has not kept pace with this shift. That gap between what the industry needs and what students are taught is part of what this project is looking to measure directly.
Retail hiring overall backs up the case for treating analytics as its own career path within the industry. The Planet Group (2025) found that retail hiring has gotten more selective even as it leans harder into technology, analytics, and customer experience. So while fewer people may be getting hired overall, the analytical roles that support pricing, inventory, operations, and customer decisions do not seem to be losing ground.
Job postings themselves give a more concrete look at what these roles ask for. Scanning ZipRecruiter listings, SQL, Excel, and a visualization tool like Tableau or Power BI show up repeatedly, alongside the usual asks for analytical and communication skills (ZipRecruiter, 2026b). We are treating this as a starting point rather than a finding, since individual job postings vary a lot by employer, seniority, and timing.
The same postings also show a fair amount of spread in pay and remote availability (ZipRecruiter, 2026a). Salary and remote work are not the central question we are asking, but they are useful context for judging how attractive a given role is. Once we are working with the MET Employability Career Match data, we will be able to check whether these early patterns hold up within our apparel retail scope specifically.
The demand for this kind of work is also reflected in national labor data. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 7% growth for market research analyst roles from 2025 to 2035 well above the average for all occupations with a median annual wage of $78,760 as of May 2025 (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). The core skills the Bureau lists are analytical thinking communication critical thinking and attention to detail and they line up closely with what the job-posting studies above describe.
Across these sources, the same picture keeps showing up: business/data analyst roles need technical skill, analytical thinking, and the ability to work with the business side, all at once. What none of this tells us yet is which of those skills matter most specifically in apparel retail, or how close our own skills already are to that bar. That gap is what this project is built to close.

title: Career Pathway and Industry Scope
text:
Target User
This product is aimed at BU MET students who are exploring analytics career paths and want a clearer picture of which industries and skills to prioritize. Our goal is to help someone in this position understand what a business/data analyst role in apparel retail actually looks like, so they can decide whether it fits their interests and know what to learn next if it does.

title: Career Evaluation
text:
Not all 19 postings in our filtered dataset represent an equally strong opportunity for this team. Some ask for skills the team already has, some are more attainable given their experience requirements, and some come from employers that are clearly hiring repeatedly for this kind of role. This page turns those factors into a scorecard so postings can be compared directly rather than assessed one at a time.
We scored each posting on three areas we have full or near-full data for across all 19 postings:

Skill fit: how many of the role’s listed skills overlap with skills the team already rates itself strong in (Data Analysis, Microsoft Excel, Stakeholder Management, and Project Management based on our skill gap findings).
Accessibility: how attainable the role is based on minimum years of experience required. A role asking for 0 years scores highest and the score drops as the experience requirement climbs.
Employer signal: how many postings from that same employer appear in our dataset as a rough proxy for how actively that company is hiring into this kind of role.

We left salary and remote status out of the combined score as only 4 of the 19 postings have that data, and folding sparse fields into a score would unfairly penalize postings that simply did not report them. We call those out separately below instead.

title: Data Preparation
text:
Note on Sample Size
The final cleaned dataset contains 19 job postings. This reflects a known limitation of NAICS-based industry classification: many analytics roles at apparel/retail companies are tagged under unrelated NAICS codes rather than under clothing retail codes specifically. To compensate, this dataset combines NAICS 458 (Clothing, Clothing Accessories, Shoe, and Jewelry Retailers) with an exact-match list of known apparel/fashion company names, then filters to narrow analyst job titles (business analyst, data analyst). The resulting sample size is small but each row is a verified, legitimate match.

title: AD688: Fashion and Apparel Career Evaluation - Group 7
text:
This project evaluates analytics-related career opportunities within the apparel and fashion industry using job-posting data from the MET Career Compass dataset.
The analysis focuses on a narrowly defined market built around NAICS 458 and a verified list of apparel and fashion employers. The current filtered dataset contains 19 job postings and is intended to provide a descriptive view of the selected market rather than represent the broader analytics labor market.

Project Sections

title: Market Baseline
text:
This page summarizes the baseline characteristics of the selected apparel and fashion analytics job market. The final filtered dataset contains 19 verified job postings based on the team’s selected NAICS 458 scope and an additional exact-match list of known apparel and fashion employers.
Because the market definition is intentionally narrow, the results should be interpreted as a descriptive snapshot of the selected apparel and fashion analytics market rather than as estimates of the broader analytics labor market.

title: Market Baseline
section: Job Volume by Title or Segment
text:
Job Volume by Title or Segment
Job titles provide an initial view of the types of analytics roles represented within the selected apparel and fashion market.


                            
                                            


The 19-posting sample contains a mix of analyst, business intelligence, ecommerce analytics, merchandise analytics, and senior analytics roles. Most job titles appear only once, suggesting that the selected market is relatively specialized and fragmented rather than concentrated around a single standardized title. A small number of titles appear more than once, but overall the postings span several analytics-related functions within apparel and fashion retail.

title: Market Baseline
text:
Functional Role Segmentation
Individual job titles in the sample are highly fragmented, with many titles appearing only once. To identify broader hiring patterns, the titles are grouped into functional categories based on the primary focus of each role. This provides a more interpretable view of the types of analytics work represented in the selected apparel and fashion job postings.


                   Functional Area  Number of Job Postings
5  Product / Engineering Analytics                       1
3             Operations Analytics                       2
4     Finance / Strategy Analytics                       2
2        Merchandising / Ecommerce                       3
1   Marketing / Customer Analytics                       5
0              BI / Data Analytics                       6

Titles classified as Other Analytics:
None


                            
                                            


The functional segmentation shows that BI and data analytics roles represent the largest share of the selected sample, with 6 of the 19 postings. Marketing and customer analytics follows closely with 5 postings, while merchandising and ecommerce account for 3. Finance and strategy analytics and operations analytics each contribute 2 postings, and product or engineering analytics contributes 1.
This broader grouping reveals that analytics hiring within the selected apparel and fashion sample is distributed across several business functions rather than being concentrated in a single type of role. Because the dataset is small and the categories are derived from job-title wording, the results should be interpreted as a descriptive view of the selected postings rather than a standardized representation of the broader industry.

title: Market Baseline
text:
Data Completeness Across Key Attributes
Several analytical fields in the job-posting dataset contain substantial missing information. Comparing attribute coverage helps distinguish which findings are supported by most of the sample and which rely on a smaller subset of postings.


               Attribute  Postings with Usable Data  Coverage Percentage
3  Observed Salary Range                          4                 21.1
5       Work Arrangement                          4                 21.1
4     Minimum Experience                          9                 47.4
0              Job Title                         19                100.0
2               Location                         19                100.0
1               Employer                         19                100.0


                            
                                            


The data-completeness analysis shows a clear difference in coverage across key job-posting attributes. Job title, employer, and location information are available for all 19 postings, while minimum-experience information is available for 9 postings. Observed salary ranges and identifiable work-arrangement information are available for only 4 postings each.
This uneven coverage is important when interpreting the EDA. Findings related to titles, employers, and geography are supported by the full sample, whereas salary, experience, and work-arrangement analyses rely on much smaller subsets of the data and should therefore be interpreted more cautiously.

title: Market Baseline
text:
Salary Distribution
Salary information is incomplete in the filtered dataset. Only postings with an originally reported salary range are included in this analysis. Missing salaries that were filled during data preparation are excluded so that the results reflect observed compensation information rather than imputed values.


Postings with observed salary ranges: 4 of 19


                            
                                            


Only 4 of the 19 postings contain an observed salary range, so the salary findings should be interpreted cautiously. The available postings show variation in both the lower and upper ends of reported compensation, but the small number of observations is not sufficient to characterize salary levels across the full selected apparel and fashion analytics market. The chart therefore presents only compensation that was explicitly reported in the source postings.

title: Market Baseline
text:
Location Patterns
Geographic information is available for most postings. A small amount of additional standardization is applied below to consolidate obvious differences in state and city labels.


                            
                                            


The 19-posting sample is concentrated in a small number of states. California and Massachusetts each account for 5 postings, followed by New York with 4 and Oregon with 3. Texas contributes 1 posting, while 1 record does not contain a usable state value. This geographic concentration appears to reflect the locations of the apparel and fashion employers represented in the filtered sample rather than a geographically representative view of the broader analytics labor market.

title: Market Baseline
text:
Experience Requirement Distribution
Experience requirements are incomplete in the source data. This analysis uses only minimum experience values that were present in the filtered dataset before missing values were filled during data preparation.


Postings with observed minimum experience requirements: 9 of 19


                            
                                            


Minimum experience information is available for 9 of the 19 postings. Among those records, 7 postings show a recorded minimum of 0 years and 2 postings show a minimum of 5 years. Because experience information is missing for more than half of the sample, these values should be interpreted as the requirements recorded in the available source data rather than as a complete representation of experience expectations across the selected market.

title: Market Baseline
text:
Remote vs Onsite Patterns
Work-arrangement information is limited in the source data. Rather than assuming that postings with missing remote-status information are onsite roles, records without a reported work arrangement are retained as a separate “Not specified” category.


Postings with an identifiable work arrangement: 4 of 19


                            
                                            


An identifiable work arrangement is available for only 4 of the 19 postings. Three postings are classified as hybrid and one as fully remote. The remaining 15 postings either do not report a work arrangement or contain an unknown value. No posting in the available sample is explicitly classified as onsite. Because work-arrangement information is unavailable for most of the sample, these results should not be used to infer the overall prevalence of remote, hybrid, or onsite work in the selected market.

title: Market Baseline
text:
Top Employers
Employer names are standardized below to consolidate obvious duplicate labels before comparing hiring activity within the selected market.


Employers represented in the sample: 8


                            
                                            


Hiring activity in the selected sample is concentrated among a small number of apparel and retail employers. Vuori and TJX each account for 5 postings, followed by Adidas with 3 and Ralph Lauren with 2. Nordstrom, Foot Locker, Michaels, and Macy’s each contribute 1 posting. These counts should be interpreted within the context of the small, intentionally filtered dataset rather than as a ranking of overall hiring activity across the apparel and fashion industry.

title: Market Baseline
text:
Baseline Summary
The market baseline provides a descriptive snapshot of analytics-related opportunities within the selected apparel and fashion industry scope. The final dataset contains 19 verified job postings and shows that analytics work appears across several functional areas, including business intelligence, merchandising, ecommerce, finance, operations, and marketing.
Hiring activity is concentrated among a small group of employers and locations. Vuori and TJX each account for 5 postings, while California and Massachusetts each account for 5 postings. New York and Oregon also represent notable hiring locations within the sample.
Several variables have substantial missing information. Only 4 postings contain observed salary ranges, 9 contain recorded minimum experience requirements, and 4 contain an identifiable work arrangement. These limitations are retained explicitly in the analysis rather than treating imputed or missing values as if they were directly reported by employers.
Overall, the findings should be interpreted as a baseline for this narrowly defined apparel and fashion analytics market rather than as estimates of the broader analytics labor market. The results provide a foundation for the later skill-gap and career-evaluation stages of the project.
